You’re surrounded by it, but do you really know and understand popular culture? What does that term even mean? This course takes a close look at popular culture past and present, introducing ways to critically analyze phenomena that coexist in our personal space daily and shape our lives, whether we want them to or not. Through a variety of critical lenses and using John Fiske's Understanding Popular Culture, we’ll examine pop culture in film and television, advertising, music, comics, gaming, and social activities such as LARP/COSplay and otaku. As a student in this seminar, you'll learn much about rhetorical strategies, critical thinking, and critical writing theory and practice. You'll produce two major pieces, a white paper and an op-ed, as well as shorter assignments designed to increase your writing knowledge and your self-awareness as a writer: keys to meeting the writing tasks in your future.

Is the book becoming obsolete? The printing press is often recognized as one of the most important inventions in human history, but has it been overshadowed by digital forms of communication? Although K-12 teachers now assign fewer full books to their students than they did in previous decades, the internet has the potential to encourage reading through avenues such as BookTok. Books can also offer a way to unplug from the digital world. In this writing seminar we will consider the long history of the book and what the format still has to offer. We will explore the wide range of books’ physical forms, from papyrus scrolls and illuminated manuscripts to mass-produced paperbacks and e-books. We will consider how books’ content is influenced by their form and the values of the cultures that produced them. We will also reflect on how our own writing fits into current trends in reading. Students will research and write papers on topics including the role of books in education, the impact of other forms of media on how we access information, and the attention economy.

Online communities are constantly generating new slang, coded phrases, and meme-based expressions that travel rapidly through algorithmic feeds. Some words go mainstream; others vanish just as quickly. Platforms act as engines of language change, shaping not only how subcultures communicate but how public conversation itself evolves — online and off. In this writing seminar, we examine how social media has become one of the most powerful forces in the creation and spread of language. We will read Adam Aleksic's Algospeak: How Social Media Is Transforming the Future of Language and use it to ask why certain phrases spread widely and how online language choices shape identity, social capital, and collective expression. Drawing on media studies, cultural history, and sociology, we will trace how algorithms influence not just which words circulate but what those words come to mean. We will analyze what happens when insider language goes mainstream, when coded speech is used to navigate moderation, and how viral phrases shift in meaning as they cross communities. Students will research and write about self-chosen issues, getting experience in the white paper and op-ed genres and the rhetoric of targeted audiences.

Everyone seems to want to belong to a vibrant community, but few people seem able to define what constitutes “community” in the first place. Furthermore, we often think of “the good life” in terms of individual happiness or success, and yet can still feel lonely no matter how accomplished we become. Perhaps the solution to these common issues is simply “figure it out together.” The central question of this seminar is How should people live together with one another? With the present rise in loneliness, social fracturing, and the loss of “third spaces” between home and work where people organically socialize, what lessons can we learn from past experiments in intentional community-building? Using Kristen Ghodsee’s book, Everyday Utopia, this seminar explores how historical, and sometimes radical, attempts at creating community can teach us what to strive for, avoid, and value as we all seek to figure out what “the good life” means for us and our communities.

Thinking about your internal experiences, perceptions, beliefs, and thoughts is a pervasive part of our everyday lives. This process of metacognition drives our ability to learn new skills, reflect on our mistakes, and so much more. Crucially, metacognition also allows us to communicate uncertainty to others and anticipate their misunderstandings. But how does metacognition actually support all of these mental feats? Can we improve our metacognitive abilities, and if so, how would we do that? In this class, we’ll read Know Thyself: The New Science of Self-Awareness by metacognition scientist Steve Fleming to answer all of these questions and more.

Who decides which voices trend and which get buried? Search engines and platforms like Threads, Instagram, TikTok, and X shape whose knowledge counts, whose communities get surveilled, and whose culture goes viral. This critical writing seminar treats digital platforms as rhetorical environments where race, gender, and power collide. Students read Safiya Umoja Noble's Algorithms of Oppression, which exposes how search engines encode racial and gender bias into their design, and examine how communities use digital spaces to organize, narrate, and claim cultural space. Students pursue independent research into a platform, hashtag campaign, algorithmic pattern, or digital community of their choosing, developed with support from a Penn Libraries research specialist. The course moves from academic argument toward public facing writing, translating research for readers such as content moderators, platform designers, journalists, digital literacy educators, and policy advocates working on questions of online bias and representation. Students complete a portfolio spanning scholarly analysis, op-ed, and public facing digital writing.

The launch of Chat GPT-3 in November 2022 and its swift integration into daily life have profoundly impacted students and educators around the world. Some educators have prohibited the use of generative AI, citing concerns of academic dishonesty and learning loss. Conversely, other educators have embraced AI, exploring its potential to enhance and enrich the learning experience. In this era of rapid AI proliferation, college students urgently need to develop AI literacy--the knowledge, skills, and abilities that enable individuals to understand, evaluate, and effectively use AI--to make informed decisions about when and how to use GenAI based on a critical assessment of its potentials and issues. This seminar will explore the emerging implications of generative technologies in postsecondary contexts from the perspective of Education, first by reading Jose Antonio Bowen and C. Edward Watson's Teaching with AI: A Practical Guide to a New Era of Human Learning. Possible topics for student projects include cheating; assessments; creativity; authorship; AI policy; field-specific uses (those in law or med school, for example); language learning; politics of access; and more. Students will compose a problem-solution white paper centered on an issue of their choice and op-ed intended for a public audience.

Do we need help choosing what to eat? How much to save for retirement? Whether to check the organ donor box at the DMV? Certain behavioral economists think so. This section will explore how everyone from city planners to nutritionists to the Internal Revenue Service engages, knowingly or not, in "choice architecture" that influences everyday decisions. Fusing behavioral economics, psychology, public policy, such "nudges" aim less to incentivize or discourage choices than gently encourage "better" habits for individuals and, in turn, society at large. This seminar will address questions of freedom, choice, and paternalism at the heart of Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sustein's bestselling book Nudge, with the broader goal of learning how we ourselves might become perceptive and influential in designed contexts we encounter each day.

This seminar considers technological systems that fail and how we might learn from such breakdowns. Defining “systems” as combinations of interdependent technologies, data analysis, and decision making that cut across technical and cultural dimensions, examples can be seen in workflows that bring new pharmaceuticals to market or patch software for airplane engines. Such accomplishments show that our increasingly technologized world has made for a standard of living inconceivable to past generations—precisely because of the complex interrelations enabled by systems. On the other hand, systems rely on connections that have resulted in failures and disasters that have left people harmed or worse. Using Meltdown: What Plane Crashes, Oil Spills, and Dumb Business Decisions Can Teach Us About How to Succeed at Work and at Home by Chris Clearfield and András Tilcsik, we will find that systems are not simply combinations of technologies: they are also embedded in social systems of people that make decisions affecting their activities and output. Students may research notable systems failures from the past, possible systems failures of the future, and how systems might best promote societal flourishing.

In this course we will look at the artistry and business acumen of Taylor Swift, and its role in fostering an enduring fan community. Through reading Crystal Haryanto’s “The Glory of Giving Everything: The Taylor Swift Business Model,” students will read Taylor Swift through multiple lenses starting with the artist as a brand creator. We seem to be living in times of uncertainty. Trying to make sense of the overlapping environmental, social, and economic crises that dominate the present moment, the simple question of “how did we get here?” can seem overwhelming. Perhaps more importantly, how do we find hope and even wonder in the world today? This seminar explores how people, power, and the environment make places what they are, for better and worse. Reading Laura Ogden’s case study of “environmental change and colonial history... in the Fuegian Archipelago of southernmost Chile and Argentina,” we will explore how people, power, and the environment interact to shape our understanding of “place.” All places are defined by their environments, the people who live there, and (increasingly) global networks of trade and power. Understanding how to make the world a better place requires first understanding how any particular place is made. As we explore place-making,” we will find areas of hope, and even wonder, that offer lessons in how people and environments can flourish despite histories of exploitation and unrelenting climate change.

In 1973, PBS began airing a daring new television program called An American Family, which anthropologist Margaret Mead speculated "may be as important for our time as were the invention of drama and the novel for earlier generations: a new way to help people understand themselves." Mead's prediction proved prescient, because An American Family ushered in a genre that, fifty years later, has proliferated globally: reality television. But to what extent is the second half of Mead's assertion true? How can shows like An American Family "help people understand themselves"? This writing seminar will explore the history of reality television and its impact on contemporary culture, within the United States and globally. Using Ruth Deller's Reality Television: The TV Phenomenon That Changed the World as our guide, we will examine how producers and consumers of reality television interpret and employ the genre as a tool to understand themselves, others, and the world.

We all know how fast fashion is a minefield of unethical labor practices, carbon emission and water pollution, and material waste at what some consider epic proportions. These are elements of the fashion industry that are visible and quantifiable. Underneath these elements reside unregulated toxic materials derived from fossil fuels that pose health risks and are likely in our wardrobes. This writing seminar will commence its study of the topic by reading and analyzing Alden Wicker's To Dye For: How Toxic Fashion Is Making Us Sick (2023). We will consider the irony of how fashion is responsible for releasing greenhouse gasses globally while its synthetic products bring autoimmune disease, infertility, asthma, and more into our own closets -- particularly those of us who are athletes, career women, flight attendants, or other uniformed students and workers. This writing seminar is transdisciplinary in nature and encourages students to research and engage with the topic in fields they find most interesting like, for example, the arts, environmentalism, legal studies, bio- and cognitive sciences, global health, and political science.

Today's musical listener has infinite access to a universe of sound, simply by pressing
"play." For much of history there was no such luxury; all music was "live" music. The
invention of recording technology fundamentally reshaped our relationship to music and
musicians, starting a trend that has culminated in the highly insulated, individualized
listening experience afforded by streaming services like Spotify. In this class we will
explore how our modern relationship to music reflects how we listen, as well as how we
value performers and composers today. Liz Pelley's recent book, Mood Machine: The
Rise of Spotify and the Costs of the Perfect Playlist, explores how the business of music
streaming reflects and shapes the modern musical landscape. The course's writing and
research assignments will enable students to explore this topic's rich, interdisciplinary
themes, while also honing their abilities to think critically and communicate with a range
of audiences.

Machine Learning and AI have grown at an enormous rate, quickly becoming something many of us interact with constantly, from our phone to asking ChatGPT for help with almost anything. Yet there is a hidden cost that we don't see: the natural resources to power computing devices, the exploited labor of workers in the industry, the source of the massive amounts of data needed, as well as the inequities ML and AI perpetuate. This writing seminar will explore this topic by starting with Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence by Kate Crawford. This will give us the background and jumping off point for our writing projects in formal or academic areas, as well as public or professional. We will develop and enhance critical reading, writing, and peer review skills as we learn about the true costs and implications of our favorite AI tools and their future incarnations.

The recent surge in right-wing populism around the world has greatly renewed interest in the forms and techniques of far-right demagoguery and mass manipulation. First systematically theorized in the 1930s to explain the mass basis of fascist movements, such techniques exploit and reinforce conformity to rigid conventionality, preoccupations with power and strength, contempt for weakness, and lack of introspection. Such characteristics provide the soil in which anti-democratic politics proliferate, which most often appeal neither to reason nor to the rational self-interest of its would-be followers but to the irrationality of strong psychological and emotional needs. What are these needs and to what extent are they socially and economically produced? To what extent is mass manipulation specific to modern political, economic, and social conditions? Is demagoguery inherent to all forms of political agitation or specific to far-right movements? Why are these politics so often accompanied by deep-seated racial prejudice and hatred that are seemingly immune to attempts to rationally dispute or disabuse? We will explore these themes through the text Prophets of Deceit: A Study of the Techniques of the American Agitator by Nobert Guterman & Leo Löwenthal. Originally published in 1949, the monograph nonetheless permits, even demands, application to the current political milieux which it anticipates with an almost clairvoyant prescience. Students will engage these ideas through a variety of assignments that develop foundational writing and analytical skills applicable to academic, professional, and public writing situations.

Sports teams, athletes, musicians, actors and other celebrities have long had fans, but in recent years, large fandoms have organized into global communities that interact online. Sometimes fandoms come to be known by their specialized names, such as Deadheads, Trekkies, Swifties, Army, Otaku, True Believers, among many others. In this writing seminar, we look into the complex psychology of fandoms, both past and present, noting both positive and negative aspects of fan behavior. We begin by reading Michael Bond’s Fans: A Journey Into the Psychology of Belonging, to understand how researchers investigate fan phenomena and describe the forces underpinning group behavior. Bond’s book is an introduction to an emerging area of research and experimentation in social psychology. Students then undertake individual research to inform their writing projects on topics related to fan behavior and group psychology.

Science fiction writers have imagined future worlds in which space travel is an everyday affair and new, often strange, religions have emerged, but have you ever really thought about religion when you think about NASA or SpaceX or Blue Origin or any of the many other organizations exploring space? Probably not. And yet, space exploration is often driven by the same fears, awe, and curiosity that drives religious seeking. We seek salvation from the mistakes we have made on earth or pursue a manifest destiny to inhabit and exploit the far reaches of the universe. This writing course will explore some of the utopian ideals and dystopian fears that dominate the corporate space race and invite us to think about the religious and ethical dimensions of space exploration. Through course reading, your own research and writing projects, and class dialogue, we will look at what our own future of space travel might hold and imagine what it might look like to explore space without reproducing the mistakes of our past.

This writing seminar focuses on a scholarly inquiry in the field of Rhetoric and Writing Studies, the study of how we use various tools--words, images, gestures, sounds, genres--to communicate with and persuade others. This seminar will introduce students to scholarly conversations on a specific topic in this discipline as a basis for understanding discipline- and profession-based writing. This includes types of reasoning, evidence, citation practices, and other means of creating, testing, and sharing knowledge with diverse audiences. Throughout, students are introduced to new writing situations as a means of sharpening their skills and learning how to be adaptive, effective writers.
Have you ever read a news article, watched a TV commercial or a music video, and wondered about its power to get into your head? This course examines how modern media engage in the rhetorical art of persuasion. Rather than focusing on social media, we'll be looking at professional media: everything from news to advertising to entertainment. We're bombarded with media rhetoric daily, and often we're aware of it as a means of manipulating our thoughts and actions, yet we consume and often succumb. We're all products of our media's unrelenting rhetorical machinations. In this seminar we'll study the rhetoric of persuasion in modern media, its historical development, and the ways it draws us into its milieu. We'll investigate how these media unite us and divide us, and hopefully come to understand them well enough to resist being pawns of the rhetoric we encounter. As a student in this seminar, you'll learn much about rhetorical strategies, critical thinking, and critical writing theory and practice. You'll produce two major pieces, a white paper and an op-ed, as well as shorter assignments designed to increase your writing knowledge and your self-awareness as a writer: keys to meeting the writing tasks in your future.

How did you decide which foods would occupy space in your refrigerator? To make this decision, you likely assessed factors like whether food items were affordable or expensive, organic or processed, and if they were craft or mass-produced. These distinctions allow us to see that the food we eat may mean more than sustenance. Thus, in this class, we will employ a sociological lens to understand the meanings we give to food. We will explore how our meanings for food allow people to do things such as develop tastes, construct identities, gain membership to gastronomic systems, and distinguish categories of people (e.g., class). As we gain a greater understanding of these food meanings, we will be able to make sense of food trends such as the rise of gourmet, organic, ethnic, and diet foods. We will read Discriminating Taste: How Class Anxiety Created the American Food Revolution by Margot Finn to understand how class serves as one of the underlying factors that inform our food meanings.

Open source software is often the hidden technology underpinning the modern world. This free sofware has its origins in the very start of modern computing and has since grown to power the internet, mobile devices, AI, and everything in between. This writing seminar will explore this topic by starting with "Working in Public: The Making and Maintenance of Open Source Software" by Nadia Asparouhova. This will give us the background and jumping off point for our writing projects, both formal or professional, as well as public. We will develop and enhance critical reading, writing, and peer review skills as we learn about the modern open source movement and the people that keep everything running.

The question "Where are you from?" evokes a myriad of responses which can vary along socio-political, economic, and cultural fault-lines. As humans, we conceptualize our identities through the meanings we attach to places. Conversely, we conceptualize place, geographically speaking, through the lenses of our identities. This phenomenon of differentiated identity mediated through place occurs at a variety of geographical and regional scales, from the local to the transnational. We may feel a sense of belonging to a country, state, city, neighborhood, or even a specific street, and therefore understand who we are in relation to that location. Using Tim Cresswell's Place: a short introduction, this course examines how space, place, and identity rhetorically interconnect as we navigate conceptual differences to arrive at shared understandings.

Open only to upperclassmen who have not fulfilled their writing requirement. These seminars follow the same curriculum as the first-year seminars but are aimed at those who have taken two or more years of college courses and are open only to juniors and seniors. The text used in these upper division sections is a highly interdisciplinary book. It allows experienced upperclassmen to find a topic of personal interest and make it their own independent research project while they continue to hone the skills that they have started to develop in college.
*This Critical Writing Seminar is part of a cluster piloting low-device classroom learning experiences. Students and faculty will engage in device-free classroom activities to facilitate community-based knowledge-building.* Everyday life depends on vast networks of pipes, cables, grids, and roadways we rarely stop to consider—until they fail. Pervasive yet out of mind, such systems route water, energy, and information while at the same time reflecting the values of the societies they sustain. Beginning with Deb Chachra's How Infrastructure Works: Inside the Systems That Shape Our World, students will investigate the relationship between infrastructure and culture, learning how the design, maintenance, or neglect of shared systems can shape communities and individual experiences. Drawing on her background in engineering and materials science, Chachra explores not only how infrastructure functions but also what it takes to maintain and reimagine such systems for more-equitable distribution of public goods. Students will choose a related research topic and engage in a series of research and writing projects organized around it, addressing issues such as aging water systems, energy scarcity, the environmental impacts of urban design, connectivity gaps, or the politics of infrastructure funding. In fulfillment of the Writing Requirement, this seminar develops essential writing skills including logical reasoning, genre analysis, research, documentation, and more. Only Juniors and Seniors who have not fulfilled their writing requirement, and Junior transfers who have not transferred writing credit from a previous institution, are eligible to enroll in Critical Composing.

Open only to sophomore transfer students who have not fulfilled their writing requirement. These seminars follow the same curriculum as the first-year seminars but are aimed at those who are transferring to Penn after completing one year of study at a previous institution. The text used in this class will be interdisciplinary and allow for broad research applications, helping sophomore transfers to find a topic of personal interest for their writing projects as they settle into a new academic environment among their peers.
This seminar, situated at the crossroads of geography, visual studies, and graphic design, re-examines how we see and navigate the world. Taking both the built environment and modes of display as sites of inquiry, together we will create new, reciprocal understandings of how culture influences place and vice versa. How do the billboards and visual communications we encounter daily shape us? How do the ways in which we move through the world impact our critical self-awareness, equipping us with the skills to solve individual and societal problems? Using the book, The Politics of the Superficial: Visual Rhetoric and the Protocol of Display, this writing seminar considers images, graphic design, and geographical-architectural analyses as key tools for communication, along with a focus on audience as a foundational concept in writing studies, and as a way of creating positive geosocial futures through rhetorical convergence.

This course is intended for capable writers who possess the maturity and temperament to work successfully as peer tutors at Penn.
Only students who have already completed the writing requirement may enroll in this course. 

The objective of this course is to prepare you to be a writing tutor. This course will advance your knowledge of writing, the field of writing studies, and how to teach and learn advanced writing skills. You will read and research a range of topics and use a variety of teaching and learning strategies: collaborative work, one-on-one peer-review; individual conferences and feedback; presentations and role-playing and, of course, writing. Another emphasis of the course is on refining your explanatory skills, from organizing your thoughts to speaking succinctly. Our course meets twice weekly, along with some hours outside of class to shadow experienced tutors as well as to do some practice tutoring yourselves.

The goal of this course is to help beginning students develop skills in Yiddish conversation, reading and writing. Yiddish is the medium of a millennium of Jewish life. We will frequently have reason to refer to the history and culture of Ashkenazie Jewry in studying the language.
In this course, you can continue to develop basic reading, writing and speaking skills. Discover treasures of Yiddish culture: songs, literature, folklore, and films.
The course will continue the first year's survey of Yiddish grammar with an additional emphasis on reading Yiddish texts. The course will also develop conversational skills in Yiddish.
Continuation of YDSH 0300. Emphasis on reading texts and conversation.

This course introduces a variety of themes and genres in Yiddish literature and culture, depending on the instructor and programmatic needs. The focus of the course may include Yiddish literature and culture in America; Yiddish literature and culture in Eastern Europe; Yiddish modernism; Art and music in the Yiddish context; Yiddish theater; Yiddish journalism; Yiddish film. Readings will be in English translation, while primary sources in Yiddish will be available, as well. Classes and coursework will be in English. There will be an optional graduate component to this course.
This course will offer a survey of the critical texts of Yiddish literature, with a particular focus on works from the early 20th century. As such, it will attend the modern literary life of Ashkenazi Jewry, working at the margins of society in the language of their community and crossing borders to create a vibrant, transnational literary culture. Students will become familiar with the major Yiddish artistic and political movements, developing an understanding of how Yiddish-language writers engaged with co-territorial and global literary cultures.
Among other themes, we’ll explore the mysticism of Hasidic tales; the moral force of the Haskalah; the experimental cosmopolitanism of Yiddish modernists; the transformation of Jewish life in the Soviet Union. We’ll hear the showtunes of New York’s Second Avenue; the ideological visions of revolutionaries and sweatshop workers; the salaciousness of “shund” (pulp or ‘trashy’) literature in the back pages of newspapers. All texts will be offered in English translation, with an optional Yiddish reading section given interest.

“Modern Jewish culture speaks with many voices,” wrote the poet, translator, and scholar Benjamin Harshav. In this course, we will echo these voices by exploring how Jewish life was shaped by cross-cultural contact and exchange with non-Jews and other Jewish communities, by studying literary manifestations of multilingualism, translation, adaptation, and circulation of texts and ideas. With a wide variety of texts - fiction, poetry, historiography, and literary criticism - from different languages and cultural contexts, this course will address several fundamental questions about, on the one hand, the ways Jews translated texts for Jewish readers, and, on the other, how Jewish experiences and traditions were translated for broader audiences. In a broader sense, we will consider what is at stake in translating Jewishness and how cultural and linguistic borders are crossed and discussed in different historical contexts.
Course assessment is comprised of two short response papers to key concepts and a literary text (with the option for a creative format), and a final paper that can be either research-based or a translation and a translator’s introduction.
All materials will be available in English but students are encouraged to read materials in their original languages if they are fluent.

The Elementary Yoruba I course can be taken to fulfill a language requirement, or for linguistic preparation to do research on Nigeria and the diaspora/Africa-related topics. The course emphasizes communicative competence to enable the students to acquire linguistic and extra-linguistic skills in Yoruba. The content of the course is selected from various everyday life situations to enable the students to communicate in predictable common daily settings. Culture, as it relates to language use, is also part of the course content. Students will acquire the speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills at the mid-high novice level, based on the ACTFL scale. The mid-high novice level proficiency skills that the students will acquire constitute threshold capabilibilities of the second semester range of proficiency to prepare students for Elementary Yoruba II course materials.

The main objective of this course is to further sharpen the Yoruba linquistic knowledge that the student acquired in level I. By the end of the course, the student should be able to (1) read, write, and understand simple to moderately complex sentences in Yoruba; and, (2) advance in the knowledge of the Yoruba culture.

This course will engage students in interpersonal and interpretive activities to enable them to satisfy most work requirements with language usage that is often, but not always, acceptable and effective. They will be able to handle with confidence, but not with facility, most normal, high-frequency social conversational situations including extensive, but casual conversations about current events, as well as work, family, and autobiographical information. Students can get the gist of most everyday conversations but has some difficulty understanding native speakers in situations that require specialized or sophisticated knowledge. Students will show considerable ability to communicate effectively on topics relating to particular interests and special fields of competence. Often, they will show a high degree of fluency and ease of speech, yet when under tension or pressure, the ability to use the language effectively may deteriorate. Comprehension of normal native speech is typically nearly complete. Typically, students with this proficiency level can participate in most social, formal, and informal interactions, but limitations either in range of contexts, types of tasks or level of accuracy hinder effectiveness.
Continuation of Intermediate I course: Level 2+ (Limited Working Proficiency, Plus)

Students will engage in interpersonal and interpretive tasks to develop productive skills to use the language with sufficient structural accuracy and vocabulary to participate effectively in most formal and informal conversations in practical, social and professional topics. Discourse will be cohesive. Students will use the language acceptably, but with some noticeable imperfections; yet, errors will never interfere with understanding and will rarely disturb the native speaker. Students will effectively combine structure and vocabulary to convey their meaning accurately, speaking readily and filling pauses suitably. In face-to-face conversation with natives speaking the standard dialect at a normal rate of speech, comprehension will be quite complete. Students can typically discuss particular interests and special fields of competence with reasonable ease. Can use the language as part of normal professional duties such as answering objections, clarifying points, justifying decisions, understanding the essence of challenges, stating and defending policy, conducting meetings, delivering briefings, or other extended and elaborate informative monologues. Can reliably elicit information and informed opinion from native speakers. Use of structural devices is flexible and elaborate. Without searching for words or phrases, students use the language clearly and relatively naturally to elaborate concepts freely and make ideas easily understandable to native speakers. Errors occur in low-frequency and highly complex structures.

This elementary course is for beginners and it requires no prior knowledge of Zulu. The course will expose students to the Zulu language and culture and will be based in the National Standards for Foreign Language Learning. Students will be engaged in communicative language learning through interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of language learning techniques. They will gain knowledge and understanding of the Zulu culture. They will use their Zulu language and culture learning experience to connect with other disciplines and further their knowledge of these disciplines through perspectives acquired from their Zulu class. They will also develop insight into the nature of language and culture through comparisons of the Zulu language and culture and their own. Through movies, songs, and other cultural activities online students will acquire the natural use of the language which will enable them to acquire linguistic and cultural skill to become life-long learners who can participate in Zulu communities in the U.S. and overseas.
